gloss: square autograph board; decorative paper board

definitions.gloss: square autograph board; decorative cardboard for writing
definitions.explanation: A stiff, square piece of decorative cardboard used for autographs, poems, calligraphy, or short messages. Commonly used in Japan to get celebrity signatures or to write farewell messages.

examples.japanese: ⟦{有名人|ゆうめいじん}→有名人：17812_yuumeijin⟧⟦に→に：00314_ni⟧{色紙|しきし}⟦に→に：00314_ni⟧⟦サイン→サイン：03846_sain⟧⟦を→を：00422_wo⟧⟦もらった→もらう：00520_morau⟧。
examples.english: I got a celebrity's autograph on a shikishi board.

examples.japanese: ⟦{退職|たいしょく}→退職：04559_taishoku⟧⟦する→する：00392_suru⟧⟦{先輩|せんぱい}→先輩：01451_senpai⟧⟦に→に：00314_ni⟧{色紙|しきし}⟦を→を：00422_wo⟧⟦{書|か}いた→書く：00477_kaku⟧。
examples.english: We wrote a farewell message on a shikishi board for our retiring senior colleague.

examples.japanese: ⟦{壁|かべ}→壁：01290_kabe⟧⟦に→に：00314_ni⟧⟦は→は：00079_ha⟧⟦プロ{野球|やきゅう}→プロ野球：08837_puroyakyuu⟧⟦{選手|せんしゅ}→選手：03823_senshu⟧⟦の→の：09472_no⟧⟦サイン→サイン：03846_sain⟧{入|い}り{色紙|しきし}⟦が→が：00051_ga⟧⟦{何枚|なんまい}→何枚：08777_nanmai⟧⟦も→も：00484_mo⟧⟦{飾|かざ}られていた→飾る：01185_kazaru⟧。
examples.english: On the wall, many autographed shikishi boards signed by professional baseball players were displayed.

notes:
READING: This entry covers the reading しきし. The same kanji {色紙|いろがみ} (read いろがみ) means "colored paper" (such as origami paper) and is a different word.

USAGE: {色紙|しきし} is a standard-sized (about 24cm × 27cm) square board. It is used in two main contexts:
1. Getting autographs from celebrities, athletes, or authors
2. Writing group farewell messages for someone leaving a workplace or school

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {色紙|しきし}⟦に→に：00314_ni⟧⟦サイン→サイン：03846_sain⟧⟦を→を：00422_wo⟧⟦もらう→もらう：00520_morau⟧ (to get an autograph on a shikishi board)
- {色紙|しきし}⟦に→に：00314_ni⟧{寄|よ}せ{書|が}き⟦を→を：00422_wo⟧⟦する→する：00392_suru⟧ (to write a group message on a shikishi board)
- ⟦サイン→サイン：03846_sain⟧{入|い}り{色紙|しきし} (autographed shikishi board)
- {色紙|しきし}⟦を→を：00422_wo⟧⟦{飾|かざ}る→飾る：01185_kazaru⟧ (to display a shikishi board)

Shikishi boards signed by famous people are often displayed in restaurants, barbershops, and offices. The {寄|よ}せ{書|が}き (group farewell message) tradition is a staple of Japanese workplace culture.
